::: {.lesson-meta}
Part 1 · Lesson 2 · About 45 minutes
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Analogy: labelled jars"}
A **value** is a thing: the number 42, the text `"engine.py"`. A **variable** is a label you stick on it so you can refer to it later. Every value also has a **type**, like the kind of jar it's in: you can add numbers, you can glue pieces of text together, but adding a number to a piece of text makes no sense, and Python will tell you so.
:::

## Variables

```python
path = "ignite/engine/engine.py"
line_number = 42
text = "    self.fire_event(Events.STARTED)"
```

`=` means "make this name refer to this value" (not "is equal to"). Names use lowercase words joined by underscores (`line_number`), a style called **snake_case**. Choose names that say what the value *means*: `line_number`, not `n`.

You can point a name at a new value at any time:

```python
count = 0
count = count + 1   # count is now 1
count += 1          # shorthand for the same thing; count is now 2
```

Anything after `#` is a **comment**: a note for humans that Python ignores.

## The basic types

| Type | Name in Python | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Whole number | `int` | `42`, `-7`, `1_000_000` |
| Decimal number | `float` | `3.5`, `0.1` |
| Text | `str` (string) | `"engine.py"`, `'hello'` |
| True or false | `bool` (boolean) | `True`, `False` |
| Nothing | `NoneType` | `None` |

`type()` tells you a value's type:

```python
print(type(path), type(line_number), type(3.5), type(True), type(None))
```
```text
<class 'str'> <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'bool'> <class 'NoneType'>
```

`None` means "no value": for example, "this file has no line count because it isn't a text file". You will see it a lot.

## Numbers and operators

```python
print(7 + 3, 7 - 3, 7 * 3, 7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ** 10)
```
```text
10 4 21 3.5 3 1 1024
```

| Operator | Means |
|---|---|
| `/` | divide, always giving a `float` |
| `//` | divide and drop the remainder |
| `%` | the remainder ("modulo"): `7 % 2` is 1, so 7 is odd |
| `**` | power |

Floats are stored in binary, so some decimals can't be represented exactly: `0.1 + 0.2` gives `0.30000000000000004`. This is true in every language. Never use floats for money; you will see the alternative when it matters.

## Strings

A string is a sequence of characters, written in single or double quotes.

```python
print(len(path))
print(path[0], path[-1], path[0:6], path[7:])
```
```text
23
i y ignite engine/engine.py
```

- `len()` gives the number of characters.
- `path[0]` is the first character: positions start at **0**. `path[-1]` is the last.
- `path[0:6]` is a **slice**: characters from position 0 up to, but not including, 6. Leave out a side to mean "from the start" or "to the end".

Strings can be joined with `+`, but the clearest way to build text from values is an **f-string**: put `f` before the quotes and variables inside `{}`.

```python
print(path + ":" + str(line_number))
print(f"{path}:{line_number}: {text.strip()}")
```
```text
ignite/engine/engine.py:42
ignite/engine/engine.py:42: self.fire_event(Events.STARTED)
```

That second line is exactly the format Atlas will print for every match: **path, line number, text**. `.strip()` removes spaces from both ends; it is a **method**, a function that belongs to a value and is called with a dot. You'll meet many string methods in lesson 1.7.

## Comparisons and booleans

Comparisons produce `True` or `False`:

```python
print(line_number > 40, line_number == 42, path != "README.md")
print("fire" in text, "Fire" in text)
```
```text
True True True
True False
```

- `==` checks equality (one `=` assigns, two compare).
- `!=` means "not equal". Also `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`.
- `in` checks whether one string appears inside another. It is **case-sensitive**: `"Fire"` is not in the text.

Combine booleans with `and`, `or` and `not`. When a condition has several parts, give each part a name: it reads like a sentence and keeps your head clear.

```python
is_python = path.endswith(".py")
is_test = path.startswith("tests/")
print(is_python and not is_test)
```
```text
True
```

## Converting between types

Python won't guess what you mean when types don't match:

```python
>>> "line " + 42
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
```

Convert explicitly:

```python
print(int("42") + 1, float("2.5"), str(7) + "7")
```
```text
43 2.5 77
```

`str(7) + "7"` is `"77"`: joining text, not adding numbers. Data from the outside world (files, the terminal, the web) always arrives as text, so you will convert often.

## In the project

Replace `main.py` in `my-atlas` with a small program that describes one search result:

```python
path = "ignite/engine/engine.py"
line_number = 890
text = "    def run("

is_python_file = path.endswith(".py")
is_inside_package = path.startswith("ignite/")

print(f"{path}:{line_number}: {text.strip()}")
print(f"Python file: {is_python_file}, part of the package: {is_inside_package}")
```

```text
$ uv run main.py
ignite/engine/engine.py:890: def run(
Python file: True, part of the package: True
```

Line 890 of Ignite's `engine.py` really is where `def run(` is (at the commit used for this course): in lesson 1.9 your program will find it by itself.

## Common mistakes

- **`=` versus `==`.** `if count = 3` is an error; comparison is `==`.
- **Forgetting the `f`** in an f-string: `"{path}"` prints the braces literally.
- **Off-by-one slicing.** The end position is excluded: `"engine"[0:3]` is `"eng"`.
- **Mixing types** without converting: `"line " + 42`.
- **Case sensitivity.** `"Events" in text` and `"events" in text` are different checks.

## Check yourself

**1.** What does `"ignite/engine.py"[-3:]` give?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`".py"`: the last three characters. A negative position counts from the end, and leaving out the end of the slice means "to the end".
:::

**2.** What are the values of `17 // 5` and `17 % 5`?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
`3` and `2`: 17 divided by 5 is 3 with remainder 2.
:::

**3.** Why does `print("count: " + count)` fail when `count` is `3`, and what are two ways to fix it?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answer"}
You can't join a `str` and an `int`. Fix with `"count: " + str(count)` or, more readably, `f"count: {count}"`.
:::

## Exercise

Given `path = "tests/ignite/metrics/test_accuracy.py"`, write a program that prints:

1. The file name only (`test_accuracy.py`), using a slice. Hint: count the characters before it, or use `path[-16:]`.
2. Whether it is a test file (starts with `tests/`) **and** a Python file, using two named booleans.
3. The line `tests/ignite/metrics/test_accuracy.py:12: def test_binary():` built with one f-string from variables.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Solution"}
```python
path = "tests/ignite/metrics/test_accuracy.py"
line_number = 12
text = "def test_binary():"

print(path[-16:])

is_test = path.startswith("tests/")
is_python = path.endswith(".py")
print(is_test and is_python)

print(f"{path}:{line_number}: {text}")
```

Counting characters by hand is fragile; in lesson 1.7 you will use `path.split("/")[-1]`, and in 1.9 `Path(path).name`, which work for any path.
:::

## Stretch

Python strings have dozens of methods. In the REPL, try `dir("text")` to list them. Find three you can guess the meaning of, try each on `"  Events.STARTED  "`, and write down what they do.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Example answer"}
`"  Events.STARTED  ".lower()` gives `'  events.started  '`; `.strip()` gives `'Events.STARTED'`; `.replace(".", "_")` gives `'  Events_STARTED  '`; `.count("E")` gives `2`. Names starting with `__` in the list are internal; ignore them for now.
:::
